contentBlocks.body: APIs often return nested data: posts that embed their author and comments, comments that embed their author. Stored as-is, the same user appears in many places, and updating their name means finding every copy. Normalizing stores each entity once, in a lookup table keyed by id, and replaces nested objects with ids.

Lookups become constant-time (users[id]), updates touch one place, and reducers stay shallow. A separate ordered id list (postIds) remembers display order, because object keys are not a reliable ordering tool.
Object keys that look like integers are always enumerated in ascending numeric order, regardless of insertion order. Keep order in an array.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why replace an embedded author object with the author's id?

choices: because JSON cannot contain nested objects
so posts can have several authors
so each user is stored once and updates happen in one place
payload.answer: so each user is stored once and updates happen in one place
payload.explanation: Duplicated copies drift out of sync; a single source per entity avoids that.
Integer-like keys come first in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order. Keys are always strings.

payload.text: A normalized users table maps each id to its record, so reading one user is a constant-time ____.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Normalize a list of posts with embedded authors and comments into postIds plus posts, comments and users tables keyed by id.
